lede: Money in a savings account, a van losing value, a population, a radioactive source: each changes by the same percentage every year, so each is multiplied by the same number every year. Repeated multiplication is a power, which is why one line of algebra and one shape of curve cover the whole family.
can: Write down the multiplier for a percentage rise or fall.
Apply it $n$ times with a power, for money, populations or decay.
Sketch $y = k^{x}$ and read growth or decay from $k$.

text: Growth, decay and the graphs of $y = k^{x}$

md: A rise of 5 per cent is not adding 5 each time; it is multiplying by 1.05 each time, and the two drift apart fast. Once you have the multiplier, four years of growth is that number to the power 4. Plot the result against the number of years and the curve is always the same shape: flat, then climbing away, or falling and flattening out.

alt: The curve y equals 2 to the power x drawn on axes from x equals 0 to 4 and y equals 0 to 16. A dot marks the point (0, 1) where the curve meets the y-axis, and the curve rises more and more steeply.
caption: Every exponential graph starts at a height of 1 and gets steeper as it goes.

prompt: A warm-up. What single number do you multiply by to increase an amount by 10 per cent?
explain: The amount keeps all of itself and gains a tenth more, so the multiplier is 1.1. Every question on this page starts with a number like that.

text: The multiplier does all the work

md:
A rise of $r$% multiplies by $1 + \frac{r}{100}$; a fall of $r$% multiplies by $1 - \frac{r}{100}$. Write that number down before anything else.

Then $n$ periods is that multiplier used $n$ times:

$$\text{value} = \text{start} \times \text{multiplier}^{\,n}$$

This is why rates cannot be added. £800 at 4% for 3 years reaches £899.89, while a single 12% rise gives only £896.

prompt: Write down the multiplier for a fall of 12 per cent.
explain: A fall of 12% leaves 88% behind, so the multiplier is 0.88. Using 0.12 instead would throw away 88% a year.

title: Why compound interest is not simple interest
md:
Simple interest gives the same number of pounds every year, because it is always $r$% of the opening balance. Compound interest gives $r$% of whatever is there **now**, and what is there now includes last year's interest.

So the yearly amounts grow, and the gap widens with every period. Over 3 years at 4%, £9000 reaches £10123.78 rather than £10080.

prompt: £5000 is put into an account paying 3% per annum compound interest. What is it worth after 4 years, to the nearest penny? Give the number of pounds.
explain: $5000 \times 1.03^{4} = 5627.5440...$, which is £5627.54. Money answers always want two decimal places.

text: The same idea as a graph

md:
Plot the value against the number of periods and you get $y = k^{x}$, where $k$ is the multiplier.

Every such curve passes through $(0, 1)$, because nothing has been multiplied yet and $k^{0} = 1$. It stays above the $x$-axis for ever: multiplying a positive number can never reach zero.

prompt: The graph of $y = k^{x}$ is drawn for some positive $k$. What is $y$ when $x = 0$?
explain: $k^{0} = 1$ whatever $k$ is. The Summer 2024 report names this one value as the mark most candidates lost on an otherwise correct exponential curve.

md:
The size of $k$ decides the shape. With $k > 1$ the curve climbs, steepening as it goes. With $0 < k < 1$ each step multiplies by less than $1$, so the curve falls and flattens out towards the axis without ever reaching it.

Run it backwards and you can read the percentage off the base: $y = 1.25^{x}$ is a rise of 25% a period, because 1.25 is $1 + 0.25$.

alt: Two curves on the same axes. One rises steeply from the point (0, 1); the other, drawn dashed and labelled k less than 1 decay, falls from (0, 1) and flattens towards the horizontal axis.
caption: Growth and decay differ only in whether the base is above or below 1. Both start at (0, 1).

prompt: A model is $y = 1.25^{x}$, with $x$ in years. What is the yearly percentage rise?
explain: Subtract the $1$ first. The extra 0.25 is the fraction gained each year, which is 25%.

title: Exponential Graphs
why: Plotting and reading exponential curves, including the shape for a base below 1. Watch it, then answer the question underneath from the picture in your head.

prompt: Which of these curves shows decay?
explain: A base between $0$ and $1$ multiplies by less than $1$ each step, so the value falls. Bases above $1$ grow.

text: Rate of change: draw the tangent

md: An exponential curve has no single gradient: it steepens at every point. So a question asking for the **rate of increase at $x = 3$** is asking for the gradient at that one point, and the only way to get it from a graph is to draw a tangent there and measure it.

prompt: Fill the gap: to show that 5 years is the **first** year past the target, you must also show the value after ______ years.
explain: Both values are needed: one shows the target has been passed, the other shows no earlier year passed it. The November 2024 report describes candidates testing only the later year and losing the mark for that reason.

md: Take the rise and the run from two points far apart on your tangent. A small triangle makes the answer depend on the thickness of your pencil.

alt: The curve y equals 2 to the power x with a straight line touching it at x equals 2, and dashed lines running across from y equals 5 to the curve and down to the horizontal axis.
caption: Two different readings: the dashed lines find an $x$ value, the touching line finds a rate of change.

prompt: A question says: by drawing a suitable line, estimate the rate of increase at $x = 3$. What is the suitable line?
options: A tangent touching the curve at $x = 3$
A straight line from the start of the curve to the point at $x = 3$
answer: A tangent touching the curve at $x = 3$
explain: The tangent's gradient is the rate of change there. The third option gives an average across the whole stretch, which for a steepening curve is a different number entirely.

title: Summer 2023 M8 Paper 2 Q11
md: A decay curve, with a reading and then a rate of decay from a tangent. Most candidates made a good attempt at the curve and the reading, and the report is blunt about the last part: the tangent needed for a rate of decay was managed only by the strongest.

prompt: Your table of values is right and your points are plotted. What still loses the last mark?
options: Joining the points with ruled straight lines
Drawing one smooth freehand curve through them
answer: Joining the points with ruled straight lines
explain: An exponential curve bends everywhere, so ruled segments are not the graph that was asked for. One smooth movement, freehand, is what the scheme wants.

title: Not on this spec
md: Logarithms appear in no CCEA GCSE Mathematics statement, so an equation like $1.25^{x} = 2$ is never solved algebraically: you read it off a graph, or you try whole numbers. Calculus is not on the specification either, which is why a rate of change is found with a drawn tangent. Continuous exponential growth using $e$ belongs to A level.

prompt: How would you solve $1.25^{x} = 2$ on this specification?
options: Read it off a drawn graph, or try whole numbers of $x$
Divide both sides by the base
answer: Read it off a drawn graph, or try whole numbers of $x$
explain: Logarithms are in no CCEA GCSE Mathematics statement, so a question of this kind always comes with a graph to read or asks only for a whole number of periods. Dividing treats the $x$ as a multiplier, which it is not.

md:
Write down the multiplier for any percentage rise or fall.
Apply it $n$ times with a power, for money, populations or decay.
Sketch $y = k^{x}$ and read growth or decay from $k$.
Estimate a rate of change on the curve by drawing a tangent.

Three or four marks on the calculator paper: a multiplier raised to a power, or a table and a curve. The first mark is the multiplier written down; the last is the value, or the first year past a target with the year on either side shown. Stuck: write the multiplier and one year of working.
